stages.name: First hour
text: Regulars. Nods, no talking. Easy money.
Bench by the shops, youngers doing loops as eyes, the little bag taped under the third slat. Slow, quiet, the way a good night starts.
First light traffic of the evening, faces you've served a hundred times, nothing above a twenty, nobody you don't already know.
fail_text: A face you don't like slows down to look twice. You call it a night early.
One of the buyers has shoes too clean for round here. He's counting, not buying, and you clock it a beat late.
The younger on the bike pedals off without a word, which is the signal, and you're already walking the other way.

stages.name: Busy
text: Word's got round. There's a queue, which is good money and bad news at the same time.
A dry spell everywhere else has sent every phone in the postcode to yours. Too much demand is its own kind of danger — a queue you can see from space.
Steady stream now, hand to hand, no gaps between them, the good rhythm where the money's coming faster than you can worry about it.
fail_text: Too many hands, too little light. One of them isn't buying.
The queue got long enough to notice and long enough to film, and one face in it was sent to make exactly that happen.
Two of them hang back instead of leaving, and men who don't leave are men waiting for something.

stages.name: The school run
text: Wrong time of day for this. Too many eyes. Too much money.
Home-time crowd, a gap in the railings the sixth-formers use, blazers with dinner money and worse ideas. The gap brings them to you, which is the only clean part.
Mums at the gates, kids everywhere, and a run of quick quiet sales in the chaos where nobody's looking at anybody for the right reasons.
fail_text: A parent's got their phone up. Not filming you. Filming near you. Close enough.
A teacher on gate duty has watched that gap in the railings all term, and today she walks over instead of writing it down.
One of the blazers is somebody's little brother and somebody's little brother is exactly who tells.

stages.name: After dark
text: Different crowd now. Bigger orders. Less chat.
Night proper now, the bench swapped for a doorway, bigger money and bigger risk and buyers who count in hundreds instead of twenties.
The evening's turned — fewer faces, deeper pockets, the kind of orders that pay for the week and attract the kind of attention that ends it.
fail_text: The bigger order comes with a bigger problem, and the problem's got mates.
A car pulls up wanting weight you don't carry on the corner, and wanting is a short step from taking.
The doorway you picked belongs to a flat whose tenant's had enough, and the door opens behind you.

stages.name: Last call
text: One car's been past three times. You've clocked it. You keep serving anyway.
Last of the night, one more sale, and a saloon that's done a slow lap of the block twice too often. You know better and you serve anyway because it's money.
You're packing up when one more face wants serving, and behind him a car sits with its lights off and its engine running.
fail_text: The car stops. The doors open on both sides. You were right about the car.
The last face wasn't buying — he was keeping you talking while the saloon came round for the third time.
Blue lights, no siren, the quiet kind that means they've been watching the whole last hour decide who you are.
